The court will hear a gerrymandering case Wednesday. Scott Bauer Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save MADISON — The Wisconsin Supreme Court will hear a gerrymandering case Wednesday that could decide if the maps for U.S. House seats should be redrawn in the state. Doug Poland, Law Forward director of litigation, and Jack Deschler of the Election Law Clinic at Harvard Law School will make oral arguments before the seven-member, liberal-leaning court. Poland and Deschler discussed the case with media across the state in a Zoom conference call. “It’s a question that is simple, but has enormous consequences for Wisconsin voters,” Poland said. “Our case is about a different kind of gerrymander. They are designed to lock in safe seats.” Wisconsin has eight U.S. House seats. Currently, Republicans hold six of the eight seats. However, Poland points out that no incumbent in Wisconsin has lost a race in the past decade, so he contends the maps are unfair because they essentially allow the congressmen to choose their voters. He said they will argue this is an “anti-competitive gerrymandering case.” The current maps “pre-ordain the elections, rather than require the candidates to run on the issues,” Poland contends. “The maps are engineered to lock in a result before Election Day.” Poland said their argument isn’t about Republican-set maps, but rather about maps that protect all incumbents. “We do not think it is true the lawsuit targets national districts,” he said. “Our challenge is based solely on Wisconsin state law.” Deschler was asked about the national implications for this case. “This is part of a national movement,” Deschler said. “We hope the Wisconsin Supreme Court will be the next step in this movement. “We’re asking for the Supreme Court to say any anti-competitive gerrymander is not allowed.” Deschler added: “We think the Wisconsin Constitution provides for this.” Poland said there is a trial date set for spring 2027 before a trial court. Any appeal would go back to the state Supreme Court. “We do think this could be resolved rather quickly,” Poland said. “We think it can be wrapped up in six or seven months.” Poland stressed that the court is not being asked to decide on the maps in this argument. “All we’re asking is the Supreme Court recognize our claim is a valid claim under state law,” Poland said. “We’re not asking the Supreme Court to do anything more than recognize our claim at this point.” He added: “We do think the court does have the authority to rule on our claim.” Deschler said the maps do not benefit one party or the other, but instead, they argue it makes all eight seats safe for the incumbents. “It’s one of the reasons we think the circuit court is fit to rule on this,” Deschler said. Poland provided a timeline for how maps could be redrawn if he wins his case. “We’d like to urge the court to rule on this very quickly, certainly by the end of the year,” Poland said. “We want to make sure we have final district in place by about April of 2028.” Deschler said that if the court agrees with them, it’s his hope that other states look at it. “We’re hoping the Wisconsin Supreme Court sets an example for other states to follow,” Deschler said.
